title: Octahedral tilting and B-site off-centering in halide perovskites are not coupled

paper_content.abstract: Metal halide perovskites show exceptional potential for solar energy, thermoelectrics, catalysis, and other photochemical technologies, with performance rooted in electronic structure-driven properties. In ABX3 halide perovskites, localized and often aspherical local electron densities from B-site lone pairs or polarizable X− anions can distort the lattice. However, the links among electronic structure fluctuations and distortions like tilting of the BX6 octahedra and off-centering of the B-site from the center of its octahedron are not fully understood. Using group theory and ab initio molecular dynamics, we quantify how lone pairs, halide polarization, off-centering, and octahedral tilting interact in the cubic phase CsBBr3, with B = Pb, Sn, and Ge. We find that lone pair-induced off-centering and octahedral tilting are symmetry-decoupled. Instead, stereochemical lone pair expression of the B-site ion is correlated to octahedral tilting through the propensity of the B-site to form a transient, partial covalent bond with the surrounding halide ions that stiffens octahedral tilting modes. These results link local electronic asymmetry to structural fluctuations and suggest that dynamic modulation of electronic symmetry offers a pathway to control functional properties in halide perovskites.
paper_content.introduction:
Lattice dynamics and their coupling to electronic structure control many important processes in metal halide perovskites. Halide perovskites exhibit soft, anharmonic phonon modes that have attracted significant interest because of their critical role in governing properties such as low thermal conductivity, dynamic disorder, carrier scattering, exciton binding and fine structure, ionic transport, and phase stability [1–10]. In cubic halide perovskites of the form ABX3, two lattice distortions that have garnered much attention are octahedral tilting [11], which occurs when alternating BX6 octahedra rotate around an axis, and off-centering of the B-site from the center of its octahedron [12].

Octahedral tilting increases the electronic gap, such that dynamic tilting increases fluctuations in the gap and alters absorption properties like the Urbach energy [11, 13–15]. Local structural changes from octahedral tilting modify orbital overlap and symmetry relevant to carrier effective masses and transport [4, 16–18]. If the B-site has a lone pair, the lone pair will localize to one side of the ion (due to s−p mixing, for example), and interactions with the surrounding halide ions produce an instability in which the B-site is displaced away from the center of the metal-halide octahedron [12, 19–24]. This off-centering, or emphanisis, significantly affects the optical properties of perovskites, such as photoluminescence [12], and can suppress their thermal conductivity [25].

Despite the importance of octahedral tilting and off-centering modes in the photophysics and thermoelectric behavior of halide perovskites, their physical origin is not fully understood, even at the level of whether or not these two modes are linked. Previous work has postulated that off-centering is coupled to octahedral tilting [26, 27]. However, a B-site lone pair and the resulting emphanisis are not a prerequisite for halide perovskites to exhibit octahedral tilting [28, 29]. Moreover, DFT calculations suggest that off-centering and octahedral tilting might even compete [30]. As a result, the question remains: how is B-site lone pair expression linked to octahedral tilting, if at all?

In this communication, we answer this question for cubic CsBBr3 perovskites using a combination of molecular dynamics simulations and group theory-based analysis of coupled electronic and nuclear fluctuations. We tune the amount of lone pair expression by varying the B-site in cubic CsBBr3 from Pb to Sn to Ge and quantify how lone pair expression couples to off-centering and octahedral tilting. By quantifying the local electronic symmetry of the B-site, we show that off-centering and octahedral tilting exhibit incommensurate symmetries, such that lone pair expression and off-centering are not directly coupled to octahedral tilting. Using the insights uncovered here by our group theory-based analysis, we suggest strategies for tuning these uncoupled low-energy instabilities in cubic halide perovskites through the local electronic structure of the component ions.
paper_content.results:
At high temperatures, ABX3 perovskites typically adopt a cubic crystal structure, Fig. 1a. However, this cubic structure is only obtained upon averaging; the instantaneous structure fluctuates away from the average cubic structure. The unstable nature of the cubic structure is evidenced by imaginary frequencies in the 0 K phonon dispersion curves [11, 31–33]. The presence of imaginary frequencies indicates mechanical instability, which, when allowed to relax, causes the perovskite to fluctuate between locally distorted states. At finite temperature, the phonon dispersion curves are renormalized by their anharmonicity, resulting in nearly flat, dispersionless bands between the M and R points in the Brillouin zone, Fig. 1b, which are attributed to octahedral tilting. Their dispersionless nature indicates localized, weakly correlated phonons [34], such that the average cubic structure emerges from the dynamical averaging of transient, locally-tilted low energy domains. This behavior is observed for CsPbBr3, CsSnBr3, and CsGeBr3, albeit with different frequencies. The frequencies of the three acoustic branches shown in Fig. 1b for all three systems are of similar frequencies for CsPbBr3 and CsSnBr3, while the frequencies of CsGeBr3 are generally higher, reflecting a stiffer crystal.

The differences among the three perovskites can in part be attributed to variations in the electronic structure of the B-site cations due to increased s−p mixing, in addition to their different sizes. To characterize the local electronic structure and its fluctuations, we use maximally localized Wannier function centers (MLWFCs) as a point representation of the electron density, which we have found to be a reasonable approximation for localized charge densities [15, 35–41]. We quantify the amount of lone pair expression through the ion-MLWFC pair distribution function, g(rdip), where rdip is the distance between the center of the ion and the MLWFC (the length of the instantaneous B-MLWFC dipole). It is clear that the width of the peak in g(rdip) increases from Pb to Sn to Ge. Additionally, the maximum in g(rdip) shifts to a non-zero value in the case of Ge, indicating substantial lone pair expression. The variation in lone pair expression among the three perovskites considered here enables us to systematically identify correlations (or lack thereof) among lone pair expression, B-site off-centering, and octahedral tilting.

The amount of lone pair expression is not the only difference between the three systems studied here; they differ in unit cell length (L) and temperature. To isolate the effects of B-site lone pair expression, we model CsPbBr3, CsSnBr3, and CsGeBr3 all at the same unit cell length, corresponding to that of cubic CsPbBr3, as well as at the same temperature of 550 K. In effect, this corresponds to modeling all three systems at the same Goldschmidt tolerance factor, t=(rCs+rBr)/(sqrt(2)(rB+rBr)), equivalent to that of CsPbBr3; ri is the radius of ion i at the state point under consideration, which is under strain for two of the three systems. The amount of lone pair expression in these model systems follows expectations, Pb < Sn < Ge, as evidenced by g(rdip), (Fig. 1c, dashed lines). In fact, the larger unit cell significantly increases the amount of lone pair expression for Sn and Ge. This is expected as lattice expansion is known to stabilize and enhance the stereochemical expression of ns2 lone pairs [5]. The qualitative trends discussed below are also exhibited by the systems at the experimentally determined unit cell size, as discussed further in the SI and shown in Fig. S4-S7, and we focus on the model systems with the same L throughout the rest of the main text unless otherwise noted.

Our quantification of octahedral tilting and off-centering is rooted in group theory, mainly using rotor functions as order parameters to quantify atomic and electronic symmetry fluctuations [15, 42, 43]. A rotor function, M_l,m = (1/N) sum_i S_l,m(Omega_i), (1) is a function of the orientation of a collection of vectors, usually around a central atom, whose value indicates how well the collective orientation overlaps with the appropriate symmetry-adapted function, S_l,m(Omega_i), which is defined by angular momentum (l) and index m, bounded by 0 <= m <= 2l, xi indicates the basis of the harmonics which here is the cubic harmonics (K), and Omega = (phi, theta) is the solid angle of each vector. The symmetry-adapted function belongs to the irreducible representation (irrep) of the site symmetry of the central atom of interest and can be used to understand group-to-subgroup transformations straightforwardly. We use these functions to quantify fluctuations in local nuclear and electronic structures accompanying octahedral tilting and B-site off-centering.

In the cubic structure, the six bromides of the BBr6 octahedron are equivalent, and distortions away from this structure reduce the number of symmetry equivalent bromides. Octahedral tilting separates the bromides into four in-plane and two axial bromides, where only the in-plane bromides participate in the rotation that results in tilting, Fig. 2a. Tilting couples to changes in the collective orientation of the bromide electron density, with the four equivalent bromides orienting an MLWFC toward the B-site. These collective fluctuations away from the average cubic structure result from the incommensurate symmetries of the site and the local electron density [15]. Octahedral tilting transforms the environment of the B-site cation from Oh to C4h, such that changes in symmetry can be monitored with an order parameter that belongs to the T1g irrep. Here, we use the rotor function M4,4 with B-Br vectors as inputs; M4,4 = 0 in the cubic structure and |M4,4| > 0 if there is octahedral tilting. The rotor function M4,4 belongs to the T1g irrep within which the B-site environment transforms upon tilting and has been shown to be a good order parameter to quantify octahedral tilting [15]. The probability distribution of this rotor function, P(M4,4), narrows when changing the B-site from Pb to Sn to Ge, which indicates decreasing amounts of octahedral tilting from CsPbBr3 to CsSnBr3 to CsGeBr3, Fig. 2b. Therefore, increasing lone pair expression from Pb to Ge appears to decrease the propensity of halide perovskites to exhibit octahedral tilting, yet the precise nature of this coupling is not known.

Stereochemical lone pair expression has been linked to off-centering of the B-site. The predominant off-centering mode is along the [111] direction, which lowers the symmetry of the B-site from Oh to C3v as it moves toward one of the faces of the Br6 octahedron [12]. This reduction in site-symmetry creates two sets of three equivalent bromides around the B-site, Fig. 2c. To quantify the amount of off-centering in each system, we computed the radial distribution function (RDF) between the position of the B-site and the center of the octahedron, g(roct), where roct = |rB - r_oct|, (2) rB is the position of the B-site cation, and r_oct is the position of the center of the octahedron. This off-centering RDF, g(roct), indicates that Pb and Sn off-center similarly, though <roct> is slightly larger with Sn, while Ge off-centers significantly further, Fig. 2d. Therefore, increasing lone pair expression, from Pb to Ge, increases the system’s propensity to undergo B-site off-centering.

Off-centering of the B-site can occur through distortions with two different symmetries. The first distortion, discussed above, lowers the B-site symmetry from Oh to C3v and corresponds to a polarization along a [111] (off-diagonal) axis. This off-diagonal mode separates the six Br ions into two groups of three equivalent Br ions that displace in opposing off-centering directions. The second distortion lowers the B-site symmetry from Oh to C4v and corresponds to polarization along a [100] (Cartesian) axis. The change in symmetry accompanying this Cartesian distortion separates the six Br ions of the octahedron into a set of four equivalent in-plane Br ions and two axial Br ions that displace in opposing directions. Based on symmetry, the Cartesian, [100] distortion is allowed to couple to octahedral tilting while the off-diagonal, [111] distortion cannot.

To quantify which polarization mode accompanies off-centering, we computed the probability as a function of the B-MLWFC vector orientation, P(Omega). To highlight the directional preferences, we show lnP(Omega) in Fig. 3, where the value of lnP(Omega) is indicated by color, and the distortion of the surface away from a sphere is proportional to P(Omega).

The lone pair of the B-site should point toward one of the faces of the BBr6 octahedron to minimize electrostatic repulsion with the bromides, and therefore we anticipate that off-centering induces polarization along the off-diagonal [111] axis. The orientational probability distributions, P(Omega), indicate that all three systems orient their B-site lone pair along the [111] axis. All probabilities exhibit minima (white) along the [100] directions and maxima (darker colors) along the [111] directions, such that orienting the B-site lone pair along the [111] direction is preferred while orienting the lone pair along [100] is unfavorable. Because we are quantifying the orientation of the B-MLWFC vector, the probability distributions also indicate that B-site off-centering must be occurring along the [111] direction and not along another axis. This preferential orientation along the [111] direction is in agreement with experimental work that attributed the asymmetry of X-ray pair distribution functions to the transient presence of rhombohedral (R3m) distortions in the average cubic perovskite structure [12]. The relatively large lone pair expression of Ge manifests in significantly larger differences in the probability distribution, as compared to the Pb and Sn systems, such that differences between the minima and maxima in P(Omega) are an order of magnitude larger in the Ge system. Overall, larger lone pair expression favors more off-centering and an increasing preference to point the lone pair toward the face of the Br6 octahedron, consistent with expectations due to minimizing electrostatic repulsions.

The incommensurate B-site symmetries of octahedral tilting and off-centering along the [111] direction suggest that lone pair expression and octahedral tilting are not correlated. To further quantify any coupling among B-site off-centering, lone pair expression, and octahedral tilting, we computed combinations of conditional probability distributions, shown in Fig. S1-S3. To illustrate the main findings, we plot the fractional deviation of various averages in Fig. 3, which are defined as chi(y) = (<x(y)>/<x>) - 1, (3) where <x(y)> = integral dx x P(x|y) and <x> = integral dy <x(y)> = integral dy integral dx x P(x|y).

We first examine chi_rdip(roct), which quantifies how the average distance between the B-site ion and its lone pair MLWFC changes with the displacement of the B-site away from its ideal position in the cubic crystal structure. We find clear correlations between rdip and roct for all three materials. However, the precise nature of the correlation is different for each, as illustrated by the quadratic fits to each data set (solid lines). When B = Pb, rdip is roughly quadratic with roct and exhibits positive curvature. When B = Ge, rdip is also quadratic with roct but exhibits negative curvature. In contrast, rdip is approximately linear with roct when B = Sn. We attribute the different trends to the different coordination environments of the B-site. For Pb, tilting dominates over off-centering, such that the coordination shell of Pb mainly consists of 4 equivalent bromides, while off-centering dominates over tilting for Ge and its coordination shell mainly has two sets of 3 equivalent bromides. Sn displays similar amounts of tilting and off-centering, such that <rdip(roct)> behaves in a manner intermediate between Pb and Ge.

Conditional averages of rdip and roct as a function of the octahedral tilting order parameter M4,4 show little to no correlation, as evidenced by chi_rdip(M4,4) and chi_roct(M4,4) in Fig. 3b, c. As a result, both stereochemical lone pair expression and off-centering are not correlated to octahedral tilting. This lack of correlation is further supported by probability distributions of the tilting order parameter conditioned on rdip or roct, which are essentially independent of lone pair expression or off-centering, Fig. S2-S3. This lack of correlation is expected from the symmetry-based arguments discussed above; tilting and ([111]) off-centering are transformations within commensurate symmetries. Because off-centering and lone pair expression are coupled, the same symmetry arguments imply that lone pair expression is also not directly coupled to octahedral tilting.

If lone pair expression and off-centering are not correlated to octahedral tilting, why does the amount of octahedral tilting decrease from Pb to Sn to Ge? The decrease in tilting results from changes in Br–B-site bonding. The differences in Br–B-site bonding can be qualitatively observed in the Br MLWF closest to the B-site. The MLWF in the Pb system exhibits minimal directionality, consistent with the small propensity for the MLWFC to align with the z-axis. In contrast, the MLWF in the Ge system exhibits a ‘teardrop’ shape consistent with partial covalent bonding between Br and Ge. The Sn system is in between these two limits.

We can quantify the changes in the local Br− electron densities through the orientational distribution functions of the bromide MLWFCs, Fig. 5d-f. For each distribution, there are two major contributions: (1) off-diagonal peaks with four-fold symmetry that are consistent with the site symmetry when tilting [15], and (2) peaks along the ±z-axis that correspond to a Br MLWFC pointing directly toward the B-site, consistent with a partial Br–B bond. From Pb to Sn to Ge, the strength of the Br–B bond increases, evidenced by the increase in the peaks along the z-direction. The high propensity for the MLWFC to align with the local z-axis and point toward a bromide in CsGeBr3 is a signature of the partial covalent bonding observed qualitatively in the MLWF isosurfaces.

The observed evolution of MLWF shape and tilt stiffness from Pb to Sn to Ge is consistent with the electronic-structure picture developed by Papoian and Hoffman: increasing s − p mixing promotes partial covalent (directional) bonding of the anion-cation pair and converts nonbonding lone pair density into bonding character, stiffening the relevant lattice modes [44–47]. The MLWF shapes we observe correspond to a continuous transition between localized lone pair character and partial multi-center bonding. This electronic transition explains the simultaneous increase in rdip and increased Br–B bonding directionality seen for Ge. This framework rationalizes why enhanced lone pair expression (larger rdip) in Ge coexists with reduced octahedral tilting; the stronger directional Br–B bonding raises the energetic cost of octahedral rotations. The observed trend in B-Br bond stiffness can also be rationalized through the lens of Hard and Soft Acid-Base (HSAB) theory [48]. The Br− anion is a borderline base while the B-site cations, Pb2+ and Sn2+, are classified as borderline soft acids due to their large size and polarizable ns2 lone pair, while the smaller Ge2+ cation is comparatively harder. The increasing B-Br bond stiffness from Pb to Ge reflects a transition from a weaker, more polarizable soft-borderline interaction to a stronger, more iono-covalent hard-borderline interaction. This provides chemical intuition for the increase in s−p mixing and partial B-Br bonding observed in Fig. 5.

Octahedral fluctuations in halide perovskites are dictated not by lone pair expression but by the strength or stiffness of the Br–B-site bond. Octahedral tilting and B-site off-centering occur in the presence of this bond, and therefore the relative propensity for either distortion is tied to the strength of the Br–B-site bond. Fluctuations between off-centering configurations require breaking this bond, and the nature and extent of octahedral tilting fluctuations are dependent on the bond strength. As a result, a dynamical competition should exist between octahedral tilting and B-site off-centering. When Br–B-site bonds are strong, as in CsGeBr3, octahedral tilting modes will be stiff. In contrast, Br–B-site bonds are weakest in CsPbBr3, and the corresponding tilting modes will be soft, while CsSnBr3 will behave in a manner between the two limits but closer to CsPbBr3.

The qualitative differences expected for the dynamics of octahedral tilting can be quantified by time correlation functions (TCFs) of a tilting order parameter [15]. We characterize fluctuations in octahedral tilting through rotation of the B-site–Br octahedron, which can be quantified by a rotor function that belongs to the T1g irrep and takes the B-Br vectors as input; M4,m with m=3,4,5. The appropriate TCF is C_tilt(t) = (<sum_m delta M4,m(0)M4,m(t)>) / (<sum_m delta M4,m(0)^2>), (4) where Gamma_tilde(l,m) is a function that returns the irrep label, Gamma(j), corresponding to each specific combination of l=4 and m, and delta_alpha,beta is the Kronecker delta function. The octahedral tilting TCF, C_tilt(t), for CsGeBr3 exhibits a rapid oscillatory decay with a deep minimum at small times. The unnormalized TCFs are also consistent with less tilting; the GeBr6 octahedra do not tilt as far as the octahedra in the other two systems, as expected from the strong Br–Ge bonds, Fig. S6.

Fluctuations in off-centering modes correspond to exchanging the identity of the (two sets of three) equivalent Br atoms around the B-site, breaking Br–B-site bonds. The large Br–Ge bond strength makes this exchange rare and slow. We characterize fluctuations in off-centering through rotation of the B-site–MLWFC dipole, which can be quantified by a rotor function that belongs to the T1u irrep and takes the B-site–MLWFC vector as input; M1,m with m = 0,1,2. We quantify the dynamics in B-site dipole rotation through a TCF analogous to that for tilting, C_dip(t) = (<sum_m delta M1,m(0)M1,m(t)>) / (<sum_m delta M1,m(0)^2>), (5) The rotational dynamics of the Ge lone pair are extremely slow, with C_dip(t) decaying on timescales of the order of tens of picoseconds, consistent with expectations. This extremely slow decay is in part due to the deep energy minima caused by the larger unit cell. Using the experimental CsGeBr3 unit cell results in a faster decay of C_dip(t), on the order of 0.5-1 ps, Fig. S5, though the dynamic competition between tilting and off-centering remains.
paper_content.methods:
Simulation Details

We performed density functional theory (DFT)-based Born-Oppenheimer ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations of CsBBr3 (B = Pb, Sn, Ge). The simulations used the QUICKSTEP electronic structure module within the CP2K ab initio code [75]. QUICKSTEP utilizes a dual atom-centered Gaussian and Plane wave (GPW) basis approach to represent wavefunctions and electron density, efficiently and precisely implementing DFT. The molecularly optimized (MOLOPT) Goedecker-Teter-Hutter (GTH) double-zeta single polarization short-ranged (DZVP-MOLOPT-SR-GTH) Gaussian basis was selected for the expansion of orbital functions. Our simulations employed a plane-wave basis with a cutoff (Ry) and a REL CUTOFF (Ry) of (400, 55), (350, 50), and (400, 50) for B = Pb, Sn, and Ge, respectively, to represent the electron density [76]. Core electrons were represented using Goedecker-Teter-Hutter (GTH) pseudopotentials [77]. Exchange correlation interactions were approximated using the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) generalized gradient approximation for the exchange-correlation functional [78], as implemented in CP2K. Grimme’s D3 van der Waals correction was applied to account for the long-range dispersion interactions in the simulations [79].

Our simulations use a 4x4x4 supercell for all perovskites based on the experimentally determined unit cells, resulting in a cubic simulation cell with lengths L = 23.80 A (Pb), 23.18 A (Sn) [80], and 22.12 A (Ge). The supercell was taken to be 4x4x4, because any odd multiple unit cells restrict octahedral tilting [81] and 2x2x2 would result in the octahedron sharing two vertexes with the same octahedron through periodic boundaries, possibly coupling these interactions more strongly. We equilibrated the system for at least 5 ps before performing production runs. These equilibration simulations propagated the equations of motion with the canonical velocity rescaling (CSVR) thermostat to maintain a constant temperature of 300 K, 450 K, 550 K for B = Sn, Pb, and Ge, respectively, for the first set of simulations in the canonical (NVT) ensemble. A second set of AIMD simulations was run so that each B-site has the unit cell of Pb and a temperature of 550 K. For the calculation of dynamic properties, we performed AIMD simulations in the microcanonical (NVE) ensemble with a timestep of 0.5 fs for a total trajectory length of at least 260 ps and 60 ps for the first and second set of simulations, respectively. Maximally localized Wannier functions (MLWFs) [82] and their centers (MLWFCs) were computed on the fly using CP2K. The spreads of the MLWFs were minimized according to established methods [83].

Phonon Analysis

To examine collective lattice dynamics by incorporating anharmonic effects at finite temperatures, we computed phonon dispersions directly from AIMD simulations. We used dump2phonon [84] to compute the dynamical matrix directly from our AIMD simulation trajectories. The elements of the dynamical matrix contain the force constants for the vibrational modes of the system. In practice, this matrix is computed within dump2phonon through Green’s functions, which involves Fourier transforms of atomic positions. The eigenvalues of the dynamical matrix give the squares of the phonon frequencies for a given wave vector. These eigenvalues were computed and the corresponding phonon dispersion curves were constructed using the phana post-processing tool [84].

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
The paper addresses the question whether octahedral tilting distortions and off-centering in halide perovskites ABX3 are
coupled to each other. Both these types of distortions play a role in the structural stability and are also occurring dynamically
at high temperature. It had been suggested in previous literature, ref. 27 in particular, that for B=Pb,Sn octahedral tilting is
favored while for B=Ge off-centering is favored although that paper already mentions that off-centering can also occur for the
Sn and Pb cases under lattice constant expansion. That paper also pointed out that the off-centering is related to lone pair
chemistry, the importance of which was previously pointed out in ref. 12. The present paper uses various sophisticated
symmetry based order parameters and statistical distribution functions to investigate the coupling or absence of coupling of
these distortion modes and their relation to lone pair expression, concepts which are here quantified precisely. The paper
concludes that these distortion modes are of different symmetry and hence uncoupled and explains the effect of lone pairs
on tilting as resulting from an indirect effect on the B-X bond stiffness resulting from the off-centering. This work clarifies the
issue of how lone-pair expression affects distortions in this family of materials. By quantifying these concepts it
puts previous assertions in literature on a firmer footing and dispels other incorrect vague assertions on the relation between
octahedral tilting to lone pair physics.
A few clarifications are required before publishing the paper and some additional suggestions below may further increase
the impact of the paper.
1) The definition of the rotor functions is somewhat incomplete, e.g. the indices ξ is not defined, I guess it relates to
irreducible representations, and Θ_i is also not defined. Relatedly, a clear explanation for why M^4,4_κ is the relevant order
parameter would be welcome. Similar for the M^1,m_κ
2) Most of the results in the main paper relate to a systems CsBBr3 all taken at fixed unit cell size of B=Pb, which means that
Sn and Ge cases are under tensile strain. The authors also provide the results for each system at their own optical lattice
constant in the supplementary information. Since expanded volume increases the lone-pair expression, as already pointed
out in ref. 27, and the authors here have a quantitative measure of lone-pair expression, can they discuss in some more
detail how the latter depends on tensile of compressive strain?
3) The authors suggest in their discussion section that replacing the B by f-electron containing elements like Eu^2+ or Yb^2+
could result in stiffening of the octahedral tilting. However, is there any evidence that these elements are compatible with the
halide perovskite structure and would have the same type of lone-pair expression? After all, the lone pairs of group IV
elements is related to the deeper s-levels in heavier elements compared to p-levels, which is, in fact due to the Darwin term
relativistic effect. Other substitutions of group II elements for the group-IV have typically led to indirect band structures and
the properties of halide perovskites are closely tied to using divalent ions of group-IV elements. The f-electrons in these
lanthanides are also quite localized and as such it is not clear what their effect in bonding would be. They might rather
introduce magnetic effects. So, this is perhaps a somewhat premature speculation, not supported by calculations.
4) Could the authors explain why the presence of flat dispersionless phonon modes along MR are indicative of octahedral
tilting. The relation of imaginary modes along this direction to the octahedral tilting were described in previous literature, e.g.
ref.29, but what is the role of the mode flatness in this context?
5) In previous literature the role of the size of the A atom in ABX3 perovskites and its relation to the Goldschmidt's tolerance
factor t was pointed out. How does this come into play in the off-centering vs. octahedral tilting question? It has been pointed
out that small t is related to tilting. Do the quantitative measures introduced here have any bearing on the role of the A size
atoms.
6) Can the analysis in terms of lone pair expression be generalized or applied also to non perovskite structures of the
halides, in which different connectivity of the octahedrons than corner sharing occurs, such as the yellow phases or
monoclinic phases. See e.g https://doi.org/10.1002/aelm.201900887.
Overall, the writing of the paper is somewhat repetitive and I think could be substantially shortened if the authors avoid
restating the same arguments at several places in the manuscript.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The authors use ab initio molecular dynamics simulations of CsBBr3 systems along with maximally localized Wannier
function analysis to address an issue about the dynamics of these systems - are B-site off-centering and octahedral tilts
coupled. The halide perovskites are a very interesting system for a variety of reasons. Many recent experimental and
theoretical works have investigated the structural transitions they display, their unusual electronic properties, their optical
properties, electronic and lattice dynamics, and the challenges to their chemical stability. Being a perovskite system, one of
the crucial coordinates governing these properties is halide octahedral tilting. Moreover, the B-site ion typically being group
14 metals, there is the interesting prospect of steric lone-pairs and their influence on properties. So the question posed by
the authors is indeed an important one for modeling these systems and also devising design principles for experiments.
The most important message from the manuscript is that, the B-site off-centering fluctuations do not couple with octahedral
tilt fluctuations since the latter are incompatible in symmetry to the (dominantly [111]) off-centering. The authors reach this
conclusion by analyzing the symmetry characters of the two kinds of fluctuations within the point-groups of the cubic (Oh)
and lowered-symmetry (C2v) structures. The same conclusion is also inferred by the lack of correlations between the two
fluctuations as obtained from the AIMD simulations. However, I am not completely convinced by this latter analysis as I
explain below.
The authors also note that the tendency for octahedral tilting decreases as the lone-pair expression increases down the
group from Ge to Sn to Pb. They attribute this to stronger s-p mixing in Ge compared to Sn and Pb and, hence, stronger B-Br
bonds. In general, this is not an original observation as it is already known that the inert pair effect, which leads to the lone
pair's inertness, increases down the group. Cation-anion interactions can result in activating the inert pair even in Pb, as in
the case of PbO (litharge) (see Journal of Solid State Chemistry 178 (2005) 1422–1428). While the authors speculate such
an s-p mixing citing some previous works (very relevant though), they do not provide an analysis confirming the same in the
systems of their focus. While tilting stiffness is shown, its connection to the involvement of valence s-orbitals from B in
bonding (through PDOS plots, for instance) is not confirmed.
Nevertheless, the connection, if it exists, shows a coupling of tilts and the extent of s-p mixing, i.e. lone-pair expression. So it
is a little confusing when a claim to the contrary is made in the manuscript.
The conditional probability analysis done on the AIMD data is used by the authors to reject the existence of a coupling
between the two features and, hence, between off-centering and tilts. Given that the lone-pair expression (x) and off-

In their paper Remsing et al are discussing the dependence of octahedral tilting in halide perovskites correlated with off
centering of the B cation and halide polarization.
Understanding these correlations is vital for the development of systematic structure to property relationships in these
materials, as these variables, or rather, their interplay are linked to key electronic properties such as the band gap that
determine their use in applications. This paper addresses this knowledge gap from a new perspective, and allows the
authors to make concrete, experimentally provable predictions. The paper is written in an very clear manner. The
conclusions are of significant importance for the field and presented in a way accessible to non-experts, which is why I
strongly recommend accepting this work.
The authors study the correlations between these variables through molecular dynamics simulations that allow them to
compute correlation functions that indicate off-centering, lone-pair expression and octahedral tilting.
Their results confirm that the width of the distribution measuring octahedral tiling increases when going from Ge to Pb,
as expected from the increase of lone pair expression in Sn and Pb.
They then move to calculate a radial distribution function between the B site position and then center of the octahedron,
which measures the B-site off centering along the [111] direction, and agrees with results from experiments. However, these
two distortions correspond to two two different distortion pathways indicated by distinct group-subgroup relationships away
from ideal octahedral symmetry, suggesting that they are uncorrelated.
The authors probe this conclusion by calculating conditional probability distributions.
These calculations indeed show that these distortions are not correlated. This result is surprising, because octahedral tilting
is usually assumed to be correlated to lone pair expression, as it increases from Ge to Pb, i.e. by increasing expression of
the lone pair.]
The authors show that this trend can be better explained by the changes in B-Br bonding, which increases from Ge to Pb.
These observations are in line with ideas proposed by Hoffman and coworkers, in which the nonbonding lone pair can mix
with p-orbitals to result in stronger directional bonding. The main result here is that fluctuations away from octahedral
symmetry are due to differences in bonding between the compounds considered here. These results are confirmed by
computing time correlation functions.

1)The plot of the log of g(r)is hard to understand for me. Is this usual to plot it like this instead of the bare function g(r) ? Do I
understand correctly that g(r) for Ge peaks at 0, while for Sn and PB the peak is nonzero, while the averages are both
nonzero? Can I understand the definition of a B-MLWFC as being equivalent to the wannier center relative to the ideal,
octahedral position in this work?
2) In general some figure captions are hard to read if not zoomed in (e.g. fig 4).Fig. 2 a little hard to identify details as well —
Could the figure be made a bit larger? The colors in Fig2. might be hard to distinguish when printed black/white.
3) The discussion about the importance of the Halide-B bond is very interesting to me. The authors discuss a plethora of
options and possible alternative B cations. Is it possible to connect the discussion here to the concept of hard acids and
bases (HSAB)? For example, the very low solubility of AgI is explained by both Ag+ and I- being soft acids/bases, resulting
in strong bonds. In contrast, AgF is highly solvable in water. This exploration would allow it to connect it to concepts more
familiar to inorganic chemists.
4) The results as they are presented are very clear and convincing, but I have trouble figuring out what implicit assumption
this analysis is based on. Are there scenarios where the authors have reason to belief their analysis is qualitatively wrong,
e.g. through change of DFT functionals or different simulation parameters. In other words, how robust are the findings and
could one easily expand it to other materials in which lone pair expression is considered to be important, e.g. Pb-based
thermoelectrics (see for example the work of Jeff Snyder).

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Metal halide perovskites show exceptional potential for solar energy, thermoelectrics, catalysis, and other photochemical technologies, with performance rooted in electronic structure-driven properties. In ABX3 halide perovskites, localized and often aspherical local electron densities from B-site lone pairs or polarizable X− anions can distort the lattice. However, the links among electronic structure fluctuations and distortions like tilting of the BX6 octahedra and off-centering of the B-site from the center of its octahedron are not fully understood. Using group theory and ab initio molecular dynamics, we quantify how lone pairs, halide polarization, off-centering, and octahedral tilting interact in the cubic phase CsBBr3, with B = Pb, Sn, and Ge. We find that lone pair-induced off-centering and octahedral tilting are symmetry-decoupled. Instead, stereochemical lone pair expression of the B-site ion is correlated to octahedral tilting through the propensity of the B-site to form a transient, partial covalent bond with the surrounding halide ions that stiffens octahedral tilting modes. These results link local electronic asymmetry to structural fluctuations and suggest that dynamic modulation of electronic symmetry offers a pathway to control functional properties in halide perovskites.

---

## Introduction

Lattice dynamics and their coupling to electronic structure control many important processes in metal halide perovskites. Halide perovskites exhibit soft, anharmonic phonon modes that have attracted significant interest because of their critical role in governing properties such as low thermal conductivity, dynamic disorder, carrier scattering, exciton binding and fine structure, ionic transport, and phase stability [1–10]. In cubic halide perovskites of the form ABX3, two lattice distortions that have garnered much attention are octahedral tilting [11], which occurs when alternating BX6 octahedra rotate around an axis, and off-centering of the B-site from the center of its octahedron [12].

Octahedral tilting increases the electronic gap, such that dynamic tilting increases fluctuations in the gap and alters absorption properties like the Urbach energy [11, 13–15]. Local structural changes from octahedral tilting modify orbital overlap and symmetry relevant to carrier effective masses and transport [4, 16–18]. If the B-site has a lone pair, the lone pair will localize to one side of the ion (due to s−p mixing, for example), and interactions with the surrounding halide ions produce an instability in which the B-site is displaced away from the center of the metal-halide octahedron [12, 19–24]. This off-centering, or emphanisis, significantly affects the optical properties of perovskites, such as photoluminescence [12], and can suppress their thermal conductivity [25].

Despite the importance of octahedral tilting and off-centering modes in the photophysics and thermoelectric behavior of halide perovskites, their physical origin is not fully understood, even at the level of whether or not these two modes are linked. Previous work has postulated that off-centering is coupled to octahedral tilting [26, 27]. However, a B-site lone pair and the resulting emphanisis are not a prerequisite for halide perovskites to exhibit octahedral tilting [28, 29]. Moreover, DFT calculations suggest that off-centering and octahedral tilting might even compete [30]. As a result, the question remains: how is B-site lone pair expression linked to octahedral tilting, if at all?

In this communication, we answer this question for cubic CsBBr3 perovskites using a combination of molecular dynamics simulations and group theory-based analysis of coupled electronic and nuclear fluctuations. We tune the amount of lone pair expression by varying the B-site in cubic CsBBr3 from Pb to Sn to Ge and quantify how lone pair expression couples to off-centering and octahedral tilting. By quantifying the local electronic symmetry of the B-site, we show that off-centering and octahedral tilting exhibit incommensurate symmetries, such that lone pair expression and off-centering are not directly coupled to octahedral tilting. Using the insights uncovered here by our group theory-based analysis, we suggest strategies for tuning these uncoupled low-energy instabilities in cubic halide perovskites through the local electronic structure of the component ions.

---

## Results

At high temperatures, ABX3 perovskites typically adopt a cubic crystal structure, Fig. 1a. However, this cubic structure is only obtained upon averaging; the instantaneous structure fluctuates away from the average cubic structure. The unstable nature of the cubic structure is evidenced by imaginary frequencies in the 0 K phonon dispersion curves [11, 31–33]. The presence of imaginary frequencies indicates mechanical instability, which, when allowed to relax, causes the perovskite to fluctuate between locally distorted states. At finite temperature, the phonon dispersion curves are renormalized by their anharmonicity, resulting in nearly flat, dispersionless bands between the M and R points in the Brillouin zone, Fig. 1b, which are attributed to octahedral tilting. Their dispersionless nature indicates localized, weakly correlated phonons [34], such that the average cubic structure emerges from the dynamical averaging of transient, locally-tilted low energy domains. This behavior is observed for CsPbBr3, CsSnBr3, and CsGeBr3, albeit with different frequencies. The frequencies of the three acoustic branches shown in Fig. 1b for all three systems are of similar frequencies for CsPbBr3 and CsSnBr3, while the frequencies of CsGeBr3 are generally higher, reflecting a stiffer crystal.

The differences among the three perovskites can in part be attributed to variations in the electronic structure of the B-site cations due to increased s−p mixing, in addition to their different sizes. To characterize the local electronic structure and its fluctuations, we use maximally localized Wannier function centers (MLWFCs) as a point representation of the electron density, which we have found to be a reasonable approximation for localized charge densities [15, 35–41]. We quantify the amount of lone pair expression through the ion-MLWFC pair distribution function, g(rdip), where rdip is the distance between the center of the ion and the MLWFC (the length of the instantaneous B-MLWFC dipole). It is clear that the width of the peak in g(rdip) increases from Pb to Sn to Ge. Additionally, the maximum in g(rdip) shifts to a non-zero value in the case of Ge, indicating substantial lone pair expression. The variation in lone pair expression among the three perovskites considered here enables us to systematically identify correlations (or lack thereof) among lone pair expression, B-site off-centering, and octahedral tilting.

The amount of lone pair expression is not the only difference between the three systems studied here; they differ in unit cell length (L) and temperature. To isolate the effects of B-site lone pair expression, we model CsPbBr3, CsSnBr3, and CsGeBr3 all at the same unit cell length, corresponding to that of cubic CsPbBr3, as well as at the same temperature of 550 K. In effect, this corresponds to modeling all three systems at the same Goldschmidt tolerance factor, t=(rCs+rBr)/(sqrt(2)(rB+rBr)), equivalent to that of CsPbBr3; ri is the radius of ion i at the state point under consideration, which is under strain for two of the three systems. The amount of lone pair expression in these model systems follows expectations, Pb < Sn < Ge, as evidenced by g(rdip), (Fig. 1c, dashed lines). In fact, the larger unit cell significantly increases the amount of lone pair expression for Sn and Ge. This is expected as lattice expansion is known to stabilize and enhance the stereochemical expression of ns2 lone pairs [5]. The qualitative trends discussed below are also exhibited by the systems at the experimentally determined unit cell size, as discussed further in the SI and shown in Fig. S4-S7, and we focus on the model systems with the same L throughout the rest of the main text unless otherwise noted.

Our quantification of octahedral tilting and off-centering is rooted in group theory, mainly using rotor functions as order parameters to quantify atomic and electronic symmetry fluctuations [15, 42, 43]. A rotor function, M_l,m = (1/N) sum_i S_l,m(Omega_i), (1) is a function of the orientation of a collection of vectors, usually around a central atom, whose value indicates how well the collective orientation overlaps with the appropriate symmetry-adapted function, S_l,m(Omega_i), which is defined by angular momentum (l) and index m, bounded by 0 <= m <= 2l, xi indicates the basis of the harmonics which here is the cubic harmonics (K), and Omega = (phi, theta) is the solid angle of each vector. The symmetry-adapted function belongs to the irreducible representation (irrep) of the site symmetry of the central atom of interest and can be used to understand group-to-subgroup transformations straightforwardly. We use these functions to quantify fluctuations in local nuclear and electronic structures accompanying octahedral tilting and B-site off-centering.

In the cubic structure, the six bromides of the BBr6 octahedron are equivalent, and distortions away from this structure reduce the number of symmetry equivalent bromides. Octahedral tilting separates the bromides into four in-plane and two axial bromides, where only the in-plane bromides participate in the rotation that results in tilting, Fig. 2a. Tilting couples to changes in the collective orientation of the bromide electron density, with the four equivalent bromides orienting an MLWFC toward the B-site. These collective fluctuations away from the average cubic structure result from the incommensurate symmetries of the site and the local electron density [15]. Octahedral tilting transforms the environment of the B-site cation from Oh to C4h, such that changes in symmetry can be monitored with an order parameter that belongs to the T1g irrep. Here, we use the rotor function M4,4 with B-Br vectors as inputs; M4,4 = 0 in the cubic structure and |M4,4| > 0 if there is octahedral tilting. The rotor function M4,4 belongs to the T1g irrep within which the B-site environment transforms upon tilting and has been shown to be a good order parameter to quantify octahedral tilting [15]. The probability distribution of this rotor function, P(M4,4), narrows when changing the B-site from Pb to Sn to Ge, which indicates decreasing amounts of octahedral tilting from CsPbBr3 to CsSnBr3 to CsGeBr3, Fig. 2b. Therefore, increasing lone pair expression from Pb to Ge appears to decrease the propensity of halide perovskites to exhibit octahedral tilting, yet the precise nature of this coupling is not known.

Stereochemical lone pair expression has been linked to off-centering of the B-site. The predominant off-centering mode is along the [111] direction, which lowers the symmetry of the B-site from Oh to C3v as it moves toward one of the faces of the Br6 octahedron [12]. This reduction in site-symmetry creates two sets of three equivalent bromides around the B-site, Fig. 2c. To quantify the amount of off-centering in each system, we computed the radial distribution function (RDF) between the position of the B-site and the center of the octahedron, g(roct), where roct = |rB - r_oct|, (2) rB is the position of the B-site cation, and r_oct is the position of the center of the octahedron. This off-centering RDF, g(roct), indicates that Pb and Sn off-center similarly, though <roct> is slightly larger with Sn, while Ge off-centers significantly further, Fig. 2d. Therefore, increasing lone pair expression, from Pb to Ge, increases the system’s propensity to undergo B-site off-centering.

Off-centering of the B-site can occur through distortions with two different symmetries. The first distortion, discussed above, lowers the B-site symmetry from Oh to C3v and corresponds to a polarization along a [111] (off-diagonal) axis. This off-diagonal mode separates the six Br ions into two groups of three equivalent Br ions that displace in opposing off-centering directions. The second distortion lowers the B-site symmetry from Oh to C4v and corresponds to polarization along a [100] (Cartesian) axis. The change in symmetry accompanying this Cartesian distortion separates the six Br ions of the octahedron into a set of four equivalent in-plane Br ions and two axial Br ions that displace in opposing directions. Based on symmetry, the Cartesian, [100] distortion is allowed to couple to octahedral tilting while the off-diagonal, [111] distortion cannot.

To quantify which polarization mode accompanies off-centering, we computed the probability as a function of the B-MLWFC vector orientation, P(Omega). To highlight the directional preferences, we show lnP(Omega) in Fig. 3, where the value of lnP(Omega) is indicated by color, and the distortion of the surface away from a sphere is proportional to P(Omega).

The lone pair of the B-site should point toward one of the faces of the BBr6 octahedron to minimize electrostatic repulsion with the bromides, and therefore we anticipate that off-centering induces polarization along the off-diagonal [111] axis. The orientational probability distributions, P(Omega), indicate that all three systems orient their B-site lone pair along the [111] axis. All probabilities exhibit minima (white) along the [100] directions and maxima (darker colors) along the [111] directions, such that orienting the B-site lone pair along the [111] direction is preferred while orienting the lone pair along [100] is unfavorable. Because we are quantifying the orientation of the B-MLWFC vector, the probability distributions also indicate that B-site off-centering must be occurring along the [111] direction and not along another axis. This preferential orientation along the [111] direction is in agreement with experimental work that attributed the asymmetry of X-ray pair distribution functions to the transient presence of rhombohedral (R3m) distortions in the average cubic perovskite structure [12]. The relatively large lone pair expression of Ge manifests in significantly larger differences in the probability distribution, as compared to the Pb and Sn systems, such that differences between the minima and maxima in P(Omega) are an order of magnitude larger in the Ge system. Overall, larger lone pair expression favors more off-centering and an increasing preference to point the lone pair toward the face of the Br6 octahedron, consistent with expectations due to minimizing electrostatic repulsions.

The incommensurate B-site symmetries of octahedral tilting and off-centering along the [111] direction suggest that lone pair expression and octahedral tilting are not correlated. To further quantify any coupling among B-site off-centering, lone pair expression, and octahedral tilting, we computed combinations of conditional probability distributions, shown in Fig. S1-S3. To illustrate the main findings, we plot the fractional deviation of various averages in Fig. 3, which are defined as chi(y) = (<x(y)>/<x>) - 1, (3) where <x(y)> = integral dx x P(x|y) and <x> = integral dy <x(y)> = integral dy integral dx x P(x|y).

We first examine chi_rdip(roct), which quantifies how the average distance between the B-site ion and its lone pair MLWFC changes with the displacement of the B-site away from its ideal position in the cubic crystal structure. We find clear correlations between rdip and roct for all three materials. However, the precise nature of the correlation is different for each, as illustrated by the quadratic fits to each data set (solid lines). When B = Pb, rdip is roughly quadratic with roct and exhibits positive curvature. When B = Ge, rdip is also quadratic with roct but exhibits negative curvature. In contrast, rdip is approximately linear with roct when B = Sn. We attribute the different trends to the different coordination environments of the B-site. For Pb, tilting dominates over off-centering, such that the coordination shell of Pb mainly consists of 4 equivalent bromides, while off-centering dominates over tilting for Ge and its coordination shell mainly has two sets of 3 equivalent bromides. Sn displays similar amounts of tilting and off-centering, such that <rdip(roct)> behaves in a manner intermediate between Pb and Ge.

Conditional averages of rdip and roct as a function of the octahedral tilting order parameter M4,4 show little to no correlation, as evidenced by chi_rdip(M4,4) and chi_roct(M4,4) in Fig. 3b, c. As a result, both stereochemical lone pair expression and off-centering are not correlated to octahedral tilting. This lack of correlation is further supported by probability distributions of the tilting order parameter conditioned on rdip or roct, which are essentially independent of lone pair expression or off-centering, Fig. S2-S3. This lack of correlation is expected from the symmetry-based arguments discussed above; tilting and ([111]) off-centering are transformations within commensurate symmetries. Because off-centering and lone pair expression are coupled, the same symmetry arguments imply that lone pair expression is also not directly coupled to octahedral tilting.

If lone pair expression and off-centering are not correlated to octahedral tilting, why does the amount of octahedral tilting decrease from Pb to Sn to Ge? The decrease in tilting results from changes in Br–B-site bonding. The differences in Br–B-site bonding can be qualitatively observed in the Br MLWF closest to the B-site. The MLWF in the Pb system exhibits minimal directionality, consistent with the small propensity for the MLWFC to align with the z-axis. In contrast, the MLWF in the Ge system exhibits a ‘teardrop’ shape consistent with partial covalent bonding between Br and Ge. The Sn system is in between these two limits.

We can quantify the changes in the local Br− electron densities through the orientational distribution functions of the bromide MLWFCs, Fig. 5d-f. For each distribution, there are two major contributions: (1) off-diagonal peaks with four-fold symmetry that are consistent with the site symmetry when tilting [15], and (2) peaks along the ±z-axis that correspond to a Br MLWFC pointing directly toward the B-site, consistent with a partial Br–B bond. From Pb to Sn to Ge, the strength of the Br–B bond increases, evidenced by the increase in the peaks along the z-direction. The high propensity for the MLWFC to align with the local z-axis and point toward a bromide in CsGeBr3 is a signature of the partial covalent bonding observed qualitatively in the MLWF isosurfaces.

The observed evolution of MLWF shape and tilt stiffness from Pb to Sn to Ge is consistent with the electronic-structure picture developed by Papoian and Hoffman: increasing s − p mixing promotes partial covalent (directional) bonding of the anion-cation pair and converts nonbonding lone pair density into bonding character, stiffening the relevant lattice modes [44–47]. The MLWF shapes we observe correspond to a continuous transition between localized lone pair character and partial multi-center bonding. This electronic transition explains the simultaneous increase in rdip and increased Br–B bonding directionality seen for Ge. This framework rationalizes why enhanced lone pair expression (larger rdip) in Ge coexists with reduced octahedral tilting; the stronger directional Br–B bonding raises the energetic cost of octahedral rotations. The observed trend in B-Br bond stiffness can also be rationalized through the lens of Hard and Soft Acid-Base (HSAB) theory [48]. The Br− anion is a borderline base while the B-site cations, Pb2+ and Sn2+, are classified as borderline soft acids due to their large size and polarizable ns2 lone pair, while the smaller Ge2+ cation is comparatively harder. The increasing B-Br bond stiffness from Pb to Ge reflects a transition from a weaker, more polarizable soft-borderline interaction to a stronger, more iono-covalent hard-borderline interaction. This provides chemical intuition for the increase in s−p mixing and partial B-Br bonding observed in Fig. 5.

Octahedral fluctuations in halide perovskites are dictated not by lone pair expression but by the strength or stiffness of the Br–B-site bond. Octahedral tilting and B-site off-centering occur in the presence of this bond, and therefore the relative propensity for either distortion is tied to the strength of the Br–B-site bond. Fluctuations between off-centering configurations require breaking this bond, and the nature and extent of octahedral tilting fluctuations are dependent on the bond strength. As a result, a dynamical competition should exist between octahedral tilting and B-site off-centering. When Br–B-site bonds are strong, as in CsGeBr3, octahedral tilting modes will be stiff. In contrast, Br–B-site bonds are weakest in CsPbBr3, and the corresponding tilting modes will be soft, while CsSnBr3 will behave in a manner between the two limits but closer to CsPbBr3.

The qualitative differences expected for the dynamics of octahedral tilting can be quantified by time correlation functions (TCFs) of a tilting order parameter [15]. We characterize fluctuations in octahedral tilting through rotation of the B-site–Br octahedron, which can be quantified by a rotor function that belongs to the T1g irrep and takes the B-Br vectors as input; M4,m with m=3,4,5. The appropriate TCF is C_tilt(t) = (<sum_m delta M4,m(0)M4,m(t)>) / (<sum_m delta M4,m(0)^2>), (4) where Gamma_tilde(l,m) is a function that returns the irrep label, Gamma(j), corresponding to each specific combination of l=4 and m, and delta_alpha,beta is the Kronecker delta function. The octahedral tilting TCF, C_tilt(t), for CsGeBr3 exhibits a rapid oscillatory decay with a deep minimum at small times. The unnormalized TCFs are also consistent with less tilting; the GeBr6 octahedra do not tilt as far as the octahedra in the other two systems, as expected from the strong Br–Ge bonds, Fig. S6.

Fluctuations in off-centering modes correspond to exchanging the identity of the (two sets of three) equivalent Br atoms around the B-site, breaking Br–B-site bonds. The large Br–Ge bond strength makes this exchange rare and slow. We characterize fluctuations in off-centering through rotation of the B-site–MLWFC dipole, which can be quantified by a rotor function that belongs to the T1u irrep and takes the B-site–MLWFC vector as input; M1,m with m = 0,1,2. We quantify the dynamics in B-site dipole rotation through a TCF analogous to that for tilting, C_dip(t) = (<sum_m delta M1,m(0)M1,m(t)>) / (<sum_m delta M1,m(0)^2>), (5) The rotational dynamics of the Ge lone pair are extremely slow, with C_dip(t) decaying on timescales of the order of tens of picoseconds, consistent with expectations. This extremely slow decay is in part due to the deep energy minima caused by the larger unit cell. Using the experimental CsGeBr3 unit cell results in a faster decay of C_dip(t), on the order of 0.5-1 ps, Fig. S5, though the dynamic competition between tilting and off-centering remains.

---

## Methods

Simulation Details

We performed density functional theory (DFT)-based Born-Oppenheimer ab initio molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations of CsBBr3 (B = Pb, Sn, Ge). The simulations used the QUICKSTEP electronic structure module within the CP2K ab initio code [75]. QUICKSTEP utilizes a dual atom-centered Gaussian and Plane wave (GPW) basis approach to represent wavefunctions and electron density, efficiently and precisely implementing DFT. The molecularly optimized (MOLOPT) Goedecker-Teter-Hutter (GTH) double-zeta single polarization short-ranged (DZVP-MOLOPT-SR-GTH) Gaussian basis was selected for the expansion of orbital functions. Our simulations employed a plane-wave basis with a cutoff (Ry) and a REL CUTOFF (Ry) of (400, 55), (350, 50), and (400, 50) for B = Pb, Sn, and Ge, respectively, to represent the electron density [76]. Core electrons were represented using Goedecker-Teter-Hutter (GTH) pseudopotentials [77]. Exchange correlation interactions were approximated using the Perdew-Burke-Ernzerhof (PBE) generalized gradient approximation for the exchange-correlation functional [78], as implemented in CP2K. Grimme’s D3 van der Waals correction was applied to account for the long-range dispersion interactions in the simulations [79].

Our simulations use a 4x4x4 supercell for all perovskites based on the experimentally determined unit cells, resulting in a cubic simulation cell with lengths L = 23.80 A (Pb), 23.18 A (Sn) [80], and 22.12 A (Ge). The supercell was taken to be 4x4x4, because any odd multiple unit cells restrict octahedral tilting [81] and 2x2x2 would result in the octahedron sharing two vertexes with the same octahedron through periodic boundaries, possibly coupling these interactions more strongly. We equilibrated the system for at least 5 ps before performing production runs. These equilibration simulations propagated the equations of motion with the canonical velocity rescaling (CSVR) thermostat to maintain a constant temperature of 300 K, 450 K, 550 K for B = Sn, Pb, and Ge, respectively, for the first set of simulations in the canonical (NVT) ensemble. A second set of AIMD simulations was run so that each B-site has the unit cell of Pb and a temperature of 550 K. For the calculation of dynamic properties, we performed AIMD simulations in the microcanonical (NVE) ensemble with a timestep of 0.5 fs for a total trajectory length of at least 260 ps and 60 ps for the first and second set of simulations, respectively. Maximally localized Wannier functions (MLWFs) [82] and their centers (MLWFCs) were computed on the fly using CP2K. The spreads of the MLWFs were minimized according to established methods [83].

Phonon Analysis

To examine collective lattice dynamics by incorporating anharmonic effects at finite temperatures, we computed phonon dispersions directly from AIMD simulations. We used dump2phonon [84] to compute the dynamical matrix directly from our AIMD simulation trajectories. The elements of the dynamical matrix contain the force constants for the vibrational modes of the system. In practice, this matrix is computed within dump2phonon through Green’s functions, which involves Fourier transforms of atomic positions. The eigenvalues of the dynamical matrix give the squares of the phonon frequencies for a given wave vector. These eigenvalues were computed and the corresponding phonon dispersion curves were constructed using the phana post-processing tool [84].

a previous study on CsSnBr3. The reason for this dominance is speculated but not clearly proved by, for instance, looking at

Overall, I feel that the main message, while interesting for researchers in the field, is not significant to appeal to a wider

combined with the group theory analysis. A more detailed discussion on the possible couplings and the corresponding free

### Reviewer 3

In their paper Remsing et al are discussing the dependence of octahedral tilting in halide perovskites correlated with off
centering of the B cation and halide polarization.
Understanding these correlations is vital for the development of systematic structure to property relationships in these
materials, as these variables, or rather, their interplay are linked to key electronic properties such as the band gap that
determine their use in applications. This paper addresses this knowledge gap from a new perspective, and allows the
authors to make concrete, experimentally provable predictions. The paper is written in an very clear manner. The
conclusions are of significant importance for the field and presented in a way accessible to non-experts, which is why I
strongly recommend accepting this work.
The authors study the correlations between these variables through molecular dynamics simulations that allow them to
compute correlation functions that indicate off-centering, lone-pair expression and octahedral tilting.
Their results confirm that the width of the distribution measuring octahedral tiling increases when going from Ge to Pb,
as expected from the increase of lone pair expression in Sn and Pb.
They then move to calculate a radial distribution function between the B site position and then center of the octahedron,
which measures the B-site off centering along the [111] direction, and agrees with results from experiments. However, these
two distortions correspond to two two different distortion pathways indicated by distinct group-subgroup relationships away
from ideal octahedral symmetry, suggesting that they are uncorrelated.
The authors probe this conclusion by calculating conditional probability distributions.
These calculations indeed show that these distortions are not correlated. This result is surprising, because octahedral tilting
is usually assumed to be correlated to lone pair expression, as it increases from Ge to Pb, i.e. by increasing expression of
the lone pair.]
The authors show that this trend can be better explained by the changes in B-Br bonding, which increases from Ge to Pb.
These observations are in line with ideas proposed by Hoffman and coworkers, in which the nonbonding lone pair can mix
with p-orbitals to result in stronger directional bonding. The main result here is that fluctuations away from octahedral
symmetry are due to differences in bonding between the compounds considered here. These results are confirmed by
computing time correlation functions.
I have a few minor questions/comments:
1)The plot of the log of g(r)is hard to understand for me. Is this usual to plot it like this instead of the bare function g(r) ? Do I
understand correctly that g(r) for Ge peaks at 0, while for Sn and PB the peak is nonzero, while the averages are both
nonzero? Can I understand the definition of a B-MLWFC as being equivalent to the wannier center relative to the ideal,
octahedral position in this work?
2) In general some figure captions are hard to read if not zoomed in (e.g. fig 4).Fig. 2 a little hard to identify details as well —
Could the figure be made a bit larger? The colors in Fig2. might be hard to distinguish when printed black/white.
3) The discussion about the importance of the Halide-B bond is very interesting to me. The authors discuss a plethora of
options and possible alternative B cations. Is it possible to connect the discussion here to the concept of hard acids and
bases (HSAB)? For example, the very low solubility of AgI is explained by both Ag+ and I- being soft acids/bases, resulting
in strong bonds. In contrast, AgF is highly solvable in water. This exploration would allow it to connect it to concepts more
familiar to inorganic chemists.
4) The results as they are presented are very clear and convincing, but I have trouble figuring out what implicit assumption
this analysis is based on. Are there scenarios where the authors have reason to belief their analysis is qualitatively wrong,
e.g. through change of DFT functionals or different simulation parameters. In other words, how robust are the findings and
could one easily expand it to other materials in which lone pair expression is considered to be important, e.g. Pb-based
